decision_reason: A1 already separates broad locomotor, stationary and upper-limb activity patterns. Its close pairs include sitting versus standing, typing versus writing, eating soup versus writing, and eating soup versus eating sandwich. Walking has the weakest supplied seen coverage, but jogging and stairs already provide meaningful locomotor anchors; adding an assumed gait distinction is not justified. Add wrist-orientation variability to distinguish local hand reorientation from global posture change, supporting transfer to typing, brushing teeth and playing catch w/tennis ball. Preserve other concepts rather than force sensor-uncertain distinctions between seated postures or individual eating activities. The supplied distances guide this refinement but do not establish recognition performance.

attributes.name: motion_intensity
attributes.definition: Overall magnitude and energy of motion within a window, including both linear and rotational components.

attributes.name: cadence
attributes.definition: Rate at which a meaningful periodic motion unit repeats over time. Cadence measures repetitions per unit time, not the total number of repetitions in the recording.

levels.Low: No clear periodic repetition or a slow repetition rate.

attributes.name: smoothness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion changes continuously rather than through sustained rapid fluctuations.

levels.Medium: Moderately smooth motion with some fluctuations.
levels.High: Continuous and smooth motion with little fluctuation.

attributes.name: impulsiveness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion contains short, abrupt, high-magnitude changes or impacts.

levels.Low: Few or no pronounced abrupt peaks.

attributes.name: posture_inclination
attributes.definition: Average gravity-relative inclination of the global load-bearing body configuration within a window, rather than the orientation of an isolated moving limb.

levels.High: Strongly inclined or nearly horizontal relative to gravity.

attributes.name: posture_variability
attributes.definition: Extent to which the global load-bearing body configuration changes relative to gravity within a window, rather than local limb-orientation changes.

attributes.name: rotational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of angular or rotational motion during the activity.

attributes.name: translational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of sustained linear progression or locomotor translation within a window.

levels.High: Prominent sustained translational or locomotor motion.

attributes.name: motion_regularity
attributes.definition: Temporal consistency and predictability of the motion pattern.

levels.Low: Irregular and poorly predictable motion pattern.
levels.Medium: Partly structured motion with moderate variability.

attributes.name: wrist_orientation_variability
attributes.definition: Extent of change in the wrist's gravity-relative orientation within a window, independent of changes in the global load-bearing body configuration.

levels.Low: Wrist orientation remains nearly constant, allowing small local adjustments.
levels.Medium: Wrist orientation changes through a moderate range.
levels.High: Wrist orientation changes through a broad range.

operations.reason: motion_intensity: G3 supports overall acceleration and rotation magnitude, retaining the walking-to-jogging transfer contrast and low-intensity typing versus vigorous ball activities. Execution effort and phone placement can blur levels; intensity alone does not identify activity.

cadence: G6 supports observable repetition rate, transferring locomotor rhythm from jogging and stairs and repetitive hand motion from clapping. This helps contrast brushing teeth with slower eating actions and dribbling (basketball) with intermittent catching. Short windows, pauses and multiple motion cycles can make the meaningful repetition unit ambiguous.

smoothness: G9 supports sustained rapid-change evidence, preserving continuous versus repeatedly fluctuating motion contrasts using writing and clapping as anchors. It remains distinct from isolated impacts. Movement speed and sensor attachment can change apparent smoothness, so no additional eating-specific distinction is imposed.

impulsiveness: G10 supports brief abrupt changes, allowing transfer from clapping and kicking (soccer ball) to ball-handling activities while distinguishing them from brushing teeth. Impacts may be attenuated or absent at the instrumented wrist; abrupt voluntary movement can also produce peaks without contact.

posture_inclination: G1 supports gravity-relative orientation when a sensor follows the load-bearing body. Retain the supplied sitting-to-standing semantic contrast without strengthening it: a user-carried phone has unspecified placement, the wrist is not a trunk proxy, and sitting need not imply trunk inclination. Its predictability is therefore conditional rather than guaranteed.

posture_variability: G12 supports changes in gravity-relative posture where sensor placement follows the body. Preserve global reconfiguration as a transfer cue from kicking (soccer ball) and folding clothes to playing catch w/tennis ball. Phone movement relative to the body and isolated arm movement can confound this evidence; the new wrist attribute must not be substituted for global posture.

rotational_motion: G2 supports angular-motion prominence from the available gyroscopes, retaining transfer from drinking from cup and eating pasta to brushing teeth and catching. Fast small rotations and slow broad rotations can have similar overall prominence; this motivates retaining a separate orientation-range concept rather than redefining this attribute.

translational_motion: G13 supports short-window translation proxies, preserving the principal locomotor bridge from jogging and stairs to walking and its contrast with stationary hand activities. These proxies do not establish absolute displacement; limb swings, integration uncertainty and phone placement limit predictability.

motion_regularity: G11 supports recurrence and temporal predictability independently of repetition speed. Jogging and clapping anchor structured walking and dribbling patterns, while folding clothes provides less regular motion. Pauses, task execution and short windows can obscure regularity; no deterministic ball-activity distinction is assumed.

wrist_orientation_variability: G12 supports gravity-relative orientation range at the wrist-worn watch, with G2 providing corroborating angular-motion evidence. Relatively stable wrist orientation during writing offers a transferable anchor for typing, while reorientation during eating soup, drinking from cup and folding clothes supports broader hand actions. This adds a plausible contrast for the close eating soup versus writing pair beyond overall intensity, and helps assess typing versus brushing teeth without equating rapid rotation with broad orientation change. Dynamic acceleration, watch alignment, technique and whether the watched hand performs the action introduce ambiguity; gravity-relative orientation also misses rotation about gravity. Do not assume it reliably separates eating soup from eating sandwich or sitting from standing.

semantic_redundancy_review: The ten attributes retain separate physical meanings: magnitude, repetition rate, sustained fluctuation, isolated peaks, global mean inclination, global posture change, angular-motion prominence, locomotor progression, temporal predictability and local wrist-orientation range. Wrist-orientation variability is spatial range rather than rotational speed or energy, and is local rather than global posture variability. Smoothness and impulsiveness may correlate but distinguish sustained fluctuations from isolated events; cadence and regularity distinguish rate from consistency. No additional dimension is introduced solely to separate closely related eating classes or sitting from standing, where the supplied sensor placement and capabilities do not justify a reliable new contrast.

_meta.validation: Semantic schema and complete A1-to-A2 lineage validated; no feature binding performed.
